Include a central tabletop with a readable chain of matched dominoes, a player's hand or tile rack, a draw pile, turn and score indicators, and a small rule or match-value cue. Make pip counts, tile orientation, and legal continuation points instantly legible. Put strong emphasis on tactile materials, strategic clarity, balanced composition, and a distinctive, professional board-game identity.

history.critique: Brief & Intent: All required modules are present (felt table, 8-tile chain, hand rack, boneyard/draw, turn pill, dual scores, match-rule row, how-to box, open-ends cue), so coverage is good — but two intent-critical legibility goals fail. The player's hand, the primary interactive surface, is rendered as dark near-black tiles with faint pips, so pip counts and legal matches cannot be read at a glance; this directly violates 'pip counts and legal continuation points instantly legible.' The LEFT/RIGHT open-end caps show only an ambiguous pip glyph with no numeral, so the '4 and 1' ends are not self-evident from the table itself (you must read the small footer text). Clarity & Hierarchy: the visual priority is inverted — the passive tabletop chain is the brightest, crispest element, while the actionable hand is the dimmest, low-contrast element; the eye goes to the wrong place. The '+4 / +8' score badges on legal tiles are useful but float over the tile top edge and never indicate WHICH end matches, so a player still has to mentally rotate each tile. The top MATCH RULE row uses tiny domino glyphs that are unreadable at that size. Visual System & Craft: the material system is split — ivory tactile tiles on the table vs. flat dark silhouettes in the hand, which reads as a half-finished state rather than an authored choice; the DISCARD tile at bottom-right is clipped at its right edge; the three bottom panels are unevenly weighted (wide hand vs. a sparse stacked right column), and the chain's per-tile tilt is slightly jittery rather than a controlled rhythm. Expressiveness & Distinctiveness: the dark-wood frame + green felt + ivory + gold palette is a strong, distinctive board-game identity, and the circular end-cap motif is a memorable idea — but the broken hand material and weak end-cap execution undercut the polish, and the boneyard '?' card and discard look generic next to the rest. Core trade-off: making the hand 'feel held' (recessed, shadowed, darker) conflicts with making its pips legible; the current draft over-prioritizes the recessed look and sacrificed readability, which is the wrong call for a strategy game where reading your hand is the whole point.
history.suggestion: Prioritized plan (offline, self-contained SVG/CSS only, no external assets): 1) UNIFY TILE MATERIAL & FIX HAND LEGIBILITY (highest impact). Re-render the 7 hand tiles in the same ivory/cream material as the tabletop chain — same pip color, same bevel, same drop shadow — and seat them in a recessed dark-wood rack with an inset shadow so they still read as 'in hand' while staying fully legible. This single change resolves the inverted hierarchy and the split material system at once. 2) MAKE OPEN ENDS SELF-EXPLANATORY. Enlarge the LEFT/RIGHT end caps into clear 'end chips' that show BOTH a numeral and the pip pattern (e.g. '4' with four pips, '1' with one pip), and color-code each chip (e.g. left = teal, right = gold) to match the turn accent. 3) STRENGTHEN LEGAL-MOVE AFFORDANCE. On the two highlighted hand tiles, keep the '+N' score badge but reposition it fully above the tile (no overlap), and add a small colored dot/arrow on the specific half of the tile that matches the corresponding open end, using the same left/right color coding from step 2 — so legality is readable without rotating the tile in your head. Add a clear hover/selected state (lift + glow) for all playable tiles. 4) FIX CRAFT/CLIPPING. Give the DISCARD tile full width so it is not cut off; replace the unreadable mini-domino glyphs in the top MATCH RULE row with small numerals or a single clear example tile; even out the three bottom panels by widening the right column or adding a subtle divider so boneyard + discard feel intentional rather than sparse. 5) AUTHOR THE CHAIN RHYTHM & FELT. Replace the jittery per-tile rotation with a consistent, deliberate tilt pattern (e.g. alternating ±2°) so the chain reads as placed-by-hand but controlled; add a faint felt vignette and a soft radial highlight under the chain to deepen the tactile table. 6) POLISH IDENTITY DETAILS. Give the boneyard a tile-stack look (layered ivory edges) instead of a flat '?' card, and ensure the '2 of 7 available' and 'Open ends' cues use the same accent colors as the end chips so the rule language and the table state visually rhyme. Sequence matters: do 1–3 first (they fix the brief's core legibility promise), then 4–6 (craft and expression), preserving every required module.
